name: Observational interpretation fallacy
statement: An association reported by an observational study is read as a causal effect, and clinical practice changes on the strength of it.
meaning: D'Amico and colleagues coined the name for a sequence they found in medical research. An observational study reports that patients who received a treatment fared better than those who did not. That comparison is read as an effect of the treatment, guidelines move, and a randomised trial run later finds no benefit or finds harm. The name labels the sequence. It is not a psychological mechanism with a measured strength, and the paper that introduced it ran no experiment on how clinicians read evidence. The statistical point beneath it is ordinary: an association can arise from chance, from bias in how the data were gathered, or from a confounder acting on both the treatment and the outcome.

origin.who: Filippo D'Amico, Marilena Marmiere, Martina Fonti, Mariarita Battaglia and Alessandro Belletti
origin.where: Journal of Evaluation in Clinical Practice
origin.note: The authors are at the department of anaesthesia and intensive care at the IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute in Milan. Their abstract states that they searched PubMed, Cochrane and Embase up to March 2024 for occasions when associations from observational studies were deemed causal, and that they found 16. The article appeared online on 29 December 2024 and in the February 2025 print issue, volume 31, issue 1, article e14288, so sources date the term to either year. Its full text is paywalled and only the abstract could be read for this entry.

evidence: The coining paper is a search of the literature for reversals, not a study of readers. Its abstract gives the databases, the March 2024 cutoff and the count of 16, and says those cases prompted revisions to clinical practice. The 16 themselves could not be read here. Two reversals of the shape it describes can be read off their own papers. Grodstein and colleagues followed 59,337 women in the Nurses' Health Study for up to 16 years and reported an adjusted relative risk of major coronary heart disease of 0.39, 95% confidence interval 0.19 to 0.78, among women taking oestrogen with progestin. The Women's Health Initiative then randomised 16,608 postmenopausal women to that combination or to placebo, and stopped the arm early after a mean of 5.2 years. Its hazard ratio for coronary heart disease was 1.29, nominal 95% confidence interval 1.02 to 1.63, on 286 cases, and its hazard ratio for stroke was 1.41, nominal 95% confidence interval 1.07 to 1.85. The Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene study randomised 29,133 Finnish male smokers aged 50 to 69, having opened by noting that diets rich in carotenoids were associated with lower lung cancer risk. Lung cancer incidence ran 18% higher among the men given beta carotene, 95% confidence interval 3 to 36%, and total mortality 8% higher, 95% confidence interval 1 to 16%. Neither pair is known to be among D'Amico and colleagues' 16, because their list could not be obtained.

replication.headline: Pooled across hundreds of topics, observational and randomised estimates agree; individual pairs diverge often enough that agreement on average is no guarantee for any one question.
replication.detail: The named fallacy has no replication record, because the paper that named it ran no experiment. The claim behind it has been tested at scale by comparing effect estimates from observational studies against randomised trials on the same question. Toews and colleagues updated the Cochrane methodological review in 2024. It covers 47 reviews and overviews, of which 34 supplied data, holding 2,869 randomised trials with 3,882,115 participants and 3,924 observational studies with 19,499,970 participants. The pooled ratio of ratios comparing randomised with observational estimates was 1.08, 95% confidence interval 1.01 to 1.15. The authors read that as no difference or a small one, rated the certainty of the evidence low, and record that 23 of the 34 reviews reported estimates in agreement on average. The 2014 version by Anglemyer, Horvath and Bero drew on 14 reviews covering 1,583 meta-analyses across 228 conditions and gave the same central figure of 1.08, 95% confidence interval 0.96 to 1.22. Earlier work points the same way. Benson and Hartz examined 136 reports on 19 treatments, and in 2 of the 19 did the pooled observational effect fall outside the 95% confidence interval of the pooled randomised effect. Concato, Shah and Horwitz compared five topics across 99 reports; for bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccine against tuberculosis, 13 randomised trials gave a relative risk of 0.49, 95% confidence interval 0.34 to 0.70, and 10 case-control studies gave an odds ratio of 0.50, 95% confidence interval 0.39 to 0.65. The disagreement sits at the level of the individual comparison. Ioannidis and colleagues took 45 topics carrying 240 randomised trials and 168 non-randomised studies. Summary odds ratios correlated at r = 0.75, and non-randomised studies tended towards larger effects, on 28 topics against 11. The two designs differed beyond chance in 7 of the 45 cases, 16%, falling to 8% among prospective studies alone, and the odds ratio varied at least twofold in 15 cases, 33%. Wang, Schneeweiss and the RCT-DUPLICATE investigators emulated 32 randomised trials in three United States claims databases, registering every protocol before analysis. Across all 32 the Pearson correlation with the trial results was 0.82, 95% confidence interval 0.64 to 0.91, with 75% agreeing on statistical significance and 66% on the estimate. For the 16 trials whose design and measurements could be emulated closely the correlation was 0.93, 95% confidence interval 0.79 to 0.97. For the 16 where it could not, it was 0.53, 95% confidence interval 0.00 to 0.83, with 56% agreeing on statistical significance and 50% on the estimate.

Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2024(1), MR000034.

limits: No figure sits in the structured effect-size fields. The Cochrane comparison reports a ratio of ratios, which is not among the metrics this site prints, and calling it an odds ratio would misstate what it measures. The count of 23,382,085 in the study field is the sum the Cochrane abstract gives for both arms of its evidence base, randomised and observational, and not a single trial population. Only the abstract of the paper that named the fallacy could be read, so its 16 cases, its definition in the authors' own words and its reference list are absent from this page. Searches of Europe PMC, Crossref and general web search for the exact phrase returned the coining paper, its English Wikipedia article and the matching Wikidata item, and nothing else. Europe PMC lists 14 papers citing the coining paper, and none of their titles indicates a study of the fallacy itself. The concordance literature answers a narrower question than the name poses. It compares pooled estimates from two study designs across many topics, and says nothing about how often a particular reader draws a causal conclusion from a single association. No experiment measuring that behaviour was located in Europe PMC, Crossref or PsycNet.
misreadings: The term looks more settled than it is. It comes from one paper published online on 29 December 2024. Its English Wikipedia article was created ten days later, on 8 January 2025, as a draft through the Article Wizard by an account named Fildam, registered at 11:38 that same morning and carrying 11 edits in total. The first author of the paper is Filippo D'Amico. The article has since taken 40 revisions, many of them bots and formatting, and it is the route by which almost all of the term's reach outside the paper travels. Beyond that page and its Wikidata item, the phrase was not found in use. A second error is to take the fallacy as the claim that observational studies overestimate treatment effects. That is the proposition Benson and Hartz and Concato and colleagues set out to test in 2000, and neither found it; the Cochrane reviews of 2014 and 2024 did not find it either. The opposite error is to read pooled agreement as permission. Ioannidis and colleagues found odds ratios varying at least twofold in a third of topics, so estimates that match on average are compatible with a particular one being far out. A fourth error is to treat the fallacy as separate from confounding. Confounding is the usual reason the causal reading is wrong, and the label names the reading rather than the mechanism, so nothing in the term tells a reader which confounder to look for.
